subject: english-language-and-literature

questions.content: What is the main aim of persuasive writing?
options: To convince the reader to agree or act
To tell a made-up story
To list facts with no opinion
To describe a place in detail
questions.explanation: Persuasive writing tries to change the reader's mind or move them to act.

questions.content: Which device is shown in: "We will not give up. We will not back down. We will not be silent."?
options: Anaphora (repetition at the start of clauses)
Simile
Onomatopoeia
Alliteration
questions.explanation: Repeating "We will not" at the start of each sentence is anaphora, which builds rhythm and emphasis.

questions.content: A rhetorical question is a question that...
options: Is asked for effect and does not expect an answer
Must be answered by the audience aloud
Is used only in poetry
Is always a mistake
questions.explanation: Rhetorical questions make readers think and often suggest the obvious answer.

questions.content: Which phrase is an example of the rule of three (a triplicate)?
options: Fast, fair and free
Fast and fair
Very very fast
Fast, but not fair
questions.explanation: The rule of three lists three items to create rhythm and a sense of completeness.

questions.content: What does emotive language aim to do?
options: Make the reader feel a strong emotion
Give exact numbers
Define a technical term
Keep the writing short
questions.explanation: Emotive words such as heartbreaking or devastating trigger feelings to support the writer's argument.

questions.content: Read this invented line from a school-lunch campaign. "Every day, thousands of hungry children sit in silence while a free meal goes in the bin." Which technique is most clearly used?
options: Emotive language and contrast
Onomatopoeia
Stage directions
Dialect
questions.explanation: Words like hungry and silence appeal to feelings, and the contrast between hungry children and wasted food strengthens the argument.

questions.content: In an invented speech, a mayor says, "Nine out of ten residents support this park." Which technique is this, and what is its purpose?
options: A statistic, used to make the claim seem factual and widely shared
A metaphor, used to describe the park
An anecdote, used to entertain
A pun, used to amuse
questions.explanation: Statistics lend authority and suggest strong support. The reader should still ask where the data came from.

questions.content: A charity advert says, "Together, we can end this." What is the effect of the pronoun "we"?
options: It creates a sense of shared purpose and includes the reader
It shows the writer is angry at the reader
It makes the sentence a question
It shows the sentence is a fact
questions.explanation: Inclusive pronouns build unity and make the audience feel part of the solution.

questions.content: Which of the following uses ethos (appeal to credibility)?
options: "As a doctor with twenty years of experience, I urge you to vaccinate."
"Think of the pain a child suffers."
"Statistics show a fall of 40%."
"Why wait? Act today!"
questions.explanation: Ethos draws on the speaker's authority or character. Pathos appeals to emotion and logos to logic.

questions.content: Which sentence best describes the effect of the hyperbole in: "This homework will take an eternity"?
options: It exaggerates to show how long and tiring the task feels
It gives an accurate time estimate
It shows the writer is calm
It shows the writer is quoting someone
questions.explanation: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis, not literal truth.

questions.content: In an invented leaflet, the writer says: "Only a fool would ignore this offer." What persuasive technique is at work?
options: Loaded language that pressures readers by insulting those who disagree
A balanced argument with both sides
A neutral statistic
A quotation from an expert
questions.explanation: Insulting an alternative viewpoint pressures readers to agree. It is manipulative rather than balanced.

questions.content: Which is the best definition of logos?
options: Appeal to reason, using facts and logical argument
Appeal to emotion
Appeal to the writer's character
Appeal to humour
questions.explanation: Logos persuades through logic, evidence and reasoning.

questions.content: A speaker says: "Some people say that recycling is pointless. But imagine our river, clean again." Why include the opposing view first?
options: To anticipate and answer a counter-argument, making the speaker seem fair and the argument stronger
To show the speaker agrees with the opposition
To make the speech longer
To show the speaker has no evidence
questions.explanation: Addressing counter-arguments can build credibility and weaken opposing positions.

questions.content: Read this invented extract. "Ask yourself: is a cheap phone worth a poisoned river? Is a bargain worth the future of our children? Of course not." What is the combined effect of the repeated rhetorical questions and the short final sentence?
options: It leads the audience to an apparently obvious conclusion and ends firmly
It confuses the audience about the topic
It makes the writing neutral
It presents the opposing view fairly
questions.explanation: The repeated questions create pattern and momentum, and the blunt answer closes down alternatives, steering the reader.

questions.content: A student writes: "The writer uses facts, so the article is unbiased." Which response is the strongest?
options: Facts can be selected and arranged to support one side, so an article can use facts and still be one-sided
Facts always make an article neutral
Bias only happens with emotive words
Articles cannot be biased
questions.explanation: Selection, omission and framing can create bias even when every individual fact is true.

questions.content: In an invented speech, a leader says, "I do not ask you to be perfect. I ask you to be present. I ask you to be brave." Which analysis is most precise?
options: Repetition of "I ask" and the shift from negative to positive create a rhythm that sounds both humble and demanding
The speaker is using onomatopoeia
The speaker uses a complex sentence
The speaker is being sarcastic
questions.explanation: Naming the technique (anaphora, contrast) and then explaining the tone and effect is the pattern of strong analysis.

questions.content: An invented advert says: "Join the thousands who have already switched." Which technique and effect are most accurate?
options: Bandwagon appeal, suggesting everyone else is doing it so the reader should too
Ethos, based on the speaker's job
Hyperbole, because thousands is a small number
A rhetorical question to avoid the topic
questions.explanation: Bandwagon appeals use popularity to pressure people to conform. The number alone does not prove the product is good.

questions.content: Which evaluation of a persuasive text shows the best critical thinking?
options: It is effective because it combines emotion with evidence, but it ignores opposing views, so a careful reader may question it
It is good because it is long
It is bad because it has emotive words
It is persuasive because the writer is certain
questions.explanation: Strong evaluation weighs strengths and weaknesses, rather than judging by length or simply labelling techniques.

note:
## Persuasion: the big idea
Persuasive and rhetorical techniques are the tools writers and speakers use to convince an audience. Rhetoric is the art of using language effectively to influence thought or action. You meet it in adverts, speeches, editorials, campaign leaflets and social media posts. To analyse it well, ask three questions: who is the audience, what does the writer want them to think or do, and how does the language help?

## The three appeals
- **Ethos** (credibility): the speaker shows they are trustworthy or expert. "As a nurse for twenty years..."
- **Pathos** (emotion): the writer stirs feelings such as pity, fear, pride or anger. "Imagine a child shivering in the cold."
- **Logos** (logic): the writer uses facts, statistics and reasoned argument. "The cost fell by forty per cent in two years."
Strong persuasion often blends all three.

## Key techniques
- **Rhetorical question**: asked for effect, not for an answer.
- **Repetition and anaphora**: repeating words at the start of clauses to build rhythm and emphasis.
- **Rule of three**: three items or phrases give a sense of completeness.
- **Emotive language**: words chosen to trigger feeling.
- **Hyperbole**: deliberate exaggeration for emphasis.
- **Direct address and inclusive pronouns**: "you" speaks to the reader; "we" builds unity.
- **Statistics and expert opinion**: add authority.
- **Anecdote**: a short personal story that makes an issue human.
- **Contrast and antithesis**: placing opposites together to sharpen a point.
- **Imperatives**: commands such as "Act now" that push the audience to respond.
- **Bandwagon appeal**: suggesting everyone else is doing it.
- **Loaded language**: words that carry judgement and push the reader towards a view.

## Analysing effects
Naming a device is not enough. Use this pattern: **technique, example, effect on audience, purpose**. For instance, in an invented campaign: "The repeated question 'Is it worth it?' pushes the reader to reject the opposing view and agree that the park should be saved." Notice how the structure of a whole text works too: it may begin with a hook, offer evidence, deal with objections, and end with a call to action.

## Thinking critically
Persuasion is not always fair. Writers can select only helpful facts, use loaded language or rely on popularity instead of proof. A good reader recognises when a technique influences them and judges whether the argument is supported by real evidence. Ask: who benefits, what is left out, and are the facts balanced?

## Common mistakes
- Spotting devices without explaining their effects.
- Saying emotive language is always bad, when it can be effective and appropriate.
- Claiming that facts make a text neutral.
- Mixing up ethos, pathos and logos.
- Ignoring audience and purpose.

## How this is examined
On-screen tasks usually give a short speech, advert or opinion extract and ask you to explain how the writer persuades the audience or evaluate how effective the text is. Multiple choice items often test whether you can name a technique accurately, link it to its effect or identify the most balanced evaluation.

Exam tip: When asked how a writer persuades, pick three techniques, quote a short example of each and explain precisely how each one affects the audience in terms of the writer's purpose.

flashcards.back: A persuasive appeal to credibility or character, such as the speaker's expertise or trustworthiness.
A persuasive appeal to emotion, such as pity, fear, pride or anger.
A persuasive appeal to logic, using facts, statistics and reasoned argument.
Repeating the same word or phrase at the start of successive sentences or clauses to build rhythm and emphasis.
A question asked for effect that does not need an answer. It invites the audience to agree.
A list of three items or phrases that creates rhythm and a feeling of completeness.
Deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis, not meant to be taken literally.
Persuading by suggesting that everyone else is doing something, so the reader should join in.

flashcards.front: How should you analyse a persuasive technique?
flashcards.back: Name it, quote an example, explain the effect on the audience and link to the writer's purpose.

subject: english-language-and-literature

questions.content: What is the purpose of a headline in a news article?
options: To summarise the story and attract the reader
To give the writer's full biography
To list all the sources
To end the article
questions.explanation: Headlines are short, attention-grabbing summaries that indicate the topic and often the angle.

questions.content: Which text type is most likely to include the writer's personal view?
options: An opinion piece
A weather report
A train timetable
A dictionary entry
questions.explanation: Opinion pieces (editorials, columns) are written to argue a point of view.

questions.content: A speech is mainly written to be...
options: Heard by an audience
Read silently
Hung on a wall
Used as a map
questions.explanation: Speeches are designed for listening, so they use repetition, direct address and clear signposting.

questions.content: What is a byline?
options: The line naming the writer of an article
The final sentence
A picture caption
A paragraph of statistics
questions.explanation: The byline credits the author, often at the start of the article.

questions.content: Which feature belongs to a formal news report?
options: Facts about who, what, where, when and why
A first-person diary tone with slang
A rhyming opening
Stage directions
questions.explanation: News reports lead with key facts, answering the main questions in the opening paragraphs.

questions.content: Read this invented opening. "Council approves £3 million for a new library after months of protest." Which feature is the sentence?
options: A news-style headline stating the key event up front
A speech opening addressing the audience
An opinion starter with a rhetorical question
A poem's title
questions.explanation: It states the central facts concisely, typical of headlines and news leads.

questions.content: An invented columnist writes: "Frankly, our so-called leaders have lost the plot." What does this tell you about the text?
options: It is an opinion piece with a strong, informal voice and loaded language
It is a neutral news report
It is a legal document
It is an instruction manual
questions.explanation: Phrases like "so-called" and "lost the plot" show judgement and a personal voice, typical of opinion writing.

questions.content: In an invented speech a student says, "Friends, classmates, teachers: look around you." Which feature is this?
options: Direct address that engages the audience and sets a collective tone
A simile
A footnote
A news lead
questions.explanation: Addressing the audience directly builds connection and attention, which is vital in speeches.

questions.content: Which feature most clearly separates a news report from an editorial?
options: The report aims to be objective, while the editorial offers an argued opinion
The report is always longer
The editorial has no headline
The report has no facts
questions.explanation: News reports aim to inform neutrally; editorials interpret and argue. Both can have headlines and facts.

questions.content: A speech repeats the phrase "This is our time." several times. Why is repetition especially useful in speeches?
options: Listeners cannot re-read, so repetition makes key ideas memorable
Speeches have no other devices
Repetition proves the facts
Speakers always run out of ideas
questions.explanation: Audiences hear a speech once, so repetition and patterns help keep ideas clear and memorable.

questions.content: An invented article reports a school's energy savings and quotes the headteacher and two students. What is the purpose of the quotations?
options: To add evidence, voices and credibility
To show the writer cannot write
To make the article shorter
To hide the facts
questions.explanation: Quotes bring in direct voices and support claims, making the report seem more reliable and human.

questions.content: Which sentence signals a balanced approach in an opinion piece?
options: "Critics have a point, yet the benefits outweigh the costs."
"Anyone who disagrees is wrong."
"This is obviously the best idea ever."
"Do as I say."
questions.explanation: Acknowledging opposing points before concluding shows balance and makes the argument more credible.

questions.content: A newspaper uses the headline "Teens Flood Town Centre" for a story about thirty students visiting a market. What does the word "flood" suggest?
options: A negative, exaggerated view that presents the group as overwhelming
A neutral, factual tone
A positive view of the visit
That the town was underwater
questions.explanation: The metaphor of a flood exaggerates the scale and may suggest a problem, showing how word choice shapes bias.

questions.content: Read this invented extract. "Three hundred people queued in the rain on Friday. They were not waiting for a concert. They were waiting for bread." What technique helps shape the reader's response?
options: Building a surprise with short sentences and a final twist that provokes sympathy
A long list of technical terms
A purely neutral statement
Slang and abbreviations
questions.explanation: The pattern of short sentences sets up an expectation and then subverts it, drawing emotion without stating it directly.

questions.content: Two invented articles report the same protest. One is headed "Peaceful march calls for safer streets", the other "Rowdy crowd blocks traffic". What is the best conclusion?
options: Word choice frames the same event differently and reveals each paper's angle
One article must be false
Headlines never influence readers
Both are identical in tone
questions.explanation: Selecting words with different connotations shapes how readers see an event, even when both articles use true details.

questions.content: A speech ends: "We began this journey together. Let us finish it together." Which analysis is strongest?
options: The repeated "together" and balanced sentences create a circular, memorable close that unites the audience
The speaker uses a metaphor about travel only
The ending is vague
The sentences are too short to matter
questions.explanation: Naming the pattern (repetition, parallelism) and explaining the effect on audience unity is stronger than a vague label.

questions.content: In an opinion piece, the writer uses first-person singular ("I"), colloquial phrases and humour. What is the likely intended effect?
options: To create a friendly, approachable voice that builds trust with readers
To make the piece sound like a legal contract
To avoid having an opinion
To make it read like a science report
questions.explanation: Informal voice builds rapport, a common aim of columns. It differs from the formal, impersonal style of reports.

questions.content: Which of these shows the best awareness of audience when writing a speech for a school assembly?
options: Using clear signposting, direct address and examples from students' own experience
Using long technical words with no explanation
Reading a dense list of figures without pauses
Speaking only to teachers
questions.explanation: A speech must suit its listeners: clear structure, direct address and relevant examples keep attention.

note:
## Three common non-fiction forms
Articles, speeches and opinion pieces are everyday forms of non-fiction. Each has its own purpose, audience and conventions. Recognising these helps you read them critically and write them convincingly.

## News articles and reports
A news report aims to inform. It usually has:
- A **headline** that summarises the story and grabs attention.
- A **byline** naming the writer.
- An **opening paragraph (lead)** answering who, what, where, when and why.
- **Details in order of importance**, with the most important facts first.
- **Quotations** from people involved, which add voices and credibility.
- A mostly **formal, third-person** style.
Even news is shaped by choices. Word choice, headline wording, which quotes are included and what is left out can create a slant.

## Features and opinion pieces
Opinion pieces, editorials and columns aim to argue or reflect. They often have:
- A **personal voice**, sometimes using "I" and humour.
- **Rhetorical devices** such as rhetorical questions, repetition and emotive language.
- **Argument structure**: hook, claim, evidence, counter-argument, conclusion.
- A **balance** of fact and opinion. Good writers acknowledge the other side before answering it.
Watch for the difference between fact (can be checked) and opinion (a judgement). Phrases such as "clearly", "surely" and "everyone knows" often disguise opinion as fact.

## Speeches
Speeches are written to be heard, so they depend on techniques that help listeners follow and remember:
- **Direct address**: "Friends, classmates..."
- **Repetition and parallel structure**: patterns that stick in memory.
- **Rule of three** and **rhetorical questions**.
- **Signposting**: "First... Second... Finally..."
- **Short sentences** for impact and a strong, memorable ending.
- A clear **call to action** or final image.
The tone should suit the occasion: a school assembly differs from a formal debate.

## Analysing audience and purpose
Always ask who the text is aimed at and why it was written. A report about a flood for a local newspaper will include local detail; a column about the same flood may blame the council. Purpose may be to inform, persuade, entertain or reflect, and many texts do more than one.

## Common mistakes
- Treating every article as neutral just because it contains facts.
- Confusing a news report with an editorial.
- Forgetting that speeches are meant to be heard, so devices of sound and repetition matter.
- Naming devices without explaining their effect on the audience.
- Ignoring headlines, which often reveal an angle.

## How this is examined
On-screen items often give a short extract from an article, speech or column and ask you to identify purpose and audience, comment on tone or explain how word choice shapes a reader's view. You may be asked to compare two accounts of the same event. Strong answers use short quotations and link them to effect.

Exam tip: Before answering, label the text type, purpose and audience in your head; then quote a specific word or phrase and explain what attitude or angle it creates.

flashcards.back: A short, attention-grabbing summary of an article's topic, often showing the paper's angle.
The line that names the writer of an article, usually at the start.
The opening of a news report that answers who, what, where, when and why, giving key facts first.
A text that argues a viewpoint, often with a personal voice, rhetoric and a balance of fact and opinion.
A fact can be checked and proved; an opinion is a personal judgement. Writers sometimes disguise opinion as fact.
Listeners hear a speech once, so repeated patterns make key ideas clear, rhythmic and memorable.
Phrases such as first, second and finally that help listeners follow the structure.

flashcards.front: How can a headline show bias?
flashcards.back: Word choice with strong connotations, such as flood or rowdy, can frame the same event positively or negatively.
Always ask who a text is for and why it was written (inform, persuade, entertain or reflect).

subject: english-language-and-literature

questions.content: What is a multimodal text?
options: A text that combines more than one mode, such as words and images
A text written in several languages only
A very long novel
A text with no images
questions.explanation: Multimodal texts use two or more modes, such as written language, images, sound, colour or layout.

questions.content: Which of these is a visual feature of a poster?
options: Colour
Rhyme
Stage direction
Footnote
questions.explanation: Colour, images, layout and font are visual features. Rhyme belongs to sound, stage directions to drama.

questions.content: What is the caption of an image?
options: Text that explains or comments on the image
The picture's frame
A hidden code
The photographer's camera
questions.explanation: Captions describe, explain or influence how we read the image.

questions.content: In design, what does layout refer to?
options: How elements are arranged on the page or screen
The colours of the author's clothes
The price of the product
The number of pages sold
questions.explanation: Layout is the arrangement of text, images and space, which guides the reader's eye.

questions.content: What does a close-up shot in an image or film usually do?
options: Draws attention to detail or emotion
Shows the entire landscape
Hides the subject
Replaces the caption
questions.explanation: Close-ups focus attention on faces or objects, highlighting feeling or importance.

questions.content: An invented poster for a water-saving campaign uses a deep blue background, a single drop in the centre, and large white text that reads: EVERY DROP COUNTS. Why might the designer place one drop in the centre?
options: To create a clear focal point that reinforces the message
To show that the poster is unfinished
To suggest there is too much water
To avoid using words
questions.explanation: A single central image creates a focal point and links directly to the slogan.

questions.content: In an invented advert, a smiling family stands in warm golden light beside a car. What is the most likely effect of the warm colours?
options: They create feelings of comfort, happiness and safety
They suggest danger
They signal the car is cheap
They make the text unreadable
questions.explanation: Warm colours are commonly linked to comfort and positive emotion, supporting the advert's message.

questions.content: A charity poster uses a photograph of a child looking directly at the viewer. What is the effect of the direct gaze?
options: It creates a personal connection and makes the viewer feel addressed
It shows the child is hiding
It shows the photo is a landscape
It makes the poster less emotional
questions.explanation: A direct gaze, called a demand image, engages the viewer and can make them feel responsible or involved.

questions.content: Which layout choice would most clearly show that a headline is the most important item?
options: Placing it at the top in large, bold type
Placing it in tiny print at the bottom
Writing it in pale grey over a busy picture
Hiding it in the middle of a paragraph
questions.explanation: Size, boldness and position at the top create hierarchy and draw attention first.

questions.content: An invented web page for a charity has red buttons labelled DONATE NOW. What is the main purpose of the colour and the imperative verb?
options: To stand out and urge immediate action
To calm the reader
To hide the donation option
To make the page slower
questions.explanation: Strong colours and imperatives are typical of calls to action, designed to prompt a click.

questions.content: A cartoon shows a giant tap pouring money into a tiny cup labelled SCHOOL. What is this technique?
options: Visual metaphor, using an image to represent an idea
Onomatopoeia
A news lead
A stage direction
questions.explanation: The image represents a larger idea (unfair funding) symbolically, which is a visual metaphor.

questions.content: A photograph taken from a low angle shows a politician standing at a podium. What impression does the low angle often give?
options: Power and authority, as the subject appears to tower over the viewer
Weakness and fear
Humour
That the picture is from the past
questions.explanation: Low-angle shots make subjects seem larger and more dominant.

questions.content: A student says, "The image and text on this poster say the same thing, so one of them is pointless." Which counter is strongest?
options: Image and words can reinforce one another, with the image giving instant emotional impact and the words giving clarity and a call to action
Words are always better
Images should never have words
Repetition is always bad
questions.explanation: Modes work together: images attract and evoke emotion, while words specify meaning and direct the reader.

questions.content: Read this invented advert. It shows a half-empty glass beside the words "Don't wait until it's gone". The glass sits against a dull grey backdrop. Which interpretation fits best?
options: The grey backdrop and half-empty glass suggest urgency and loss to push the viewer to act
The grey backdrop signals celebration
The glass shows the product is overflowing
The text means the viewer should relax
questions.explanation: Muted colours and the image of something running out support an urgent call to action.

questions.content: An invented cereal advert shows children laughing in a bright kitchen, with small text at the bottom reading "Contains 30% sugar". What can a critical reader conclude about the design?
options: Positive imagery dominates the page while a less flattering fact is made small and easy to miss
The advert is hiding the product
All the text is the same size
The advert contains no persuasion
questions.explanation: Hierarchy of size and placement guides attention. Critical readers notice what is emphasised and what is minimised.

questions.content: Which analysis of a poster's colour scheme is the strongest?
options: The cool blues and greens link to nature and calm, supporting the poster's environmental theme and making the red slogan stand out by contrast
The poster uses colours
Blue is a nice colour
Green is the writer's favourite colour
questions.explanation: Strong analysis names the colours, links them to associations and explains how they support meaning or emphasis.

questions.content: In an invented film poster, the hero stands small at the bottom while a huge storm cloud fills the top two-thirds of the frame. What is the most likely message?
options: The hero faces overwhelming odds
The hero is in complete control
The film is a documentary about weather
The film is a comedy about umbrellas
questions.explanation: Scale and composition show relative power. A small figure under a looming cloud suggests vulnerability and challenge.

questions.content: A news website shows a close-up of a crying protester above an article titled "Protest ends peacefully". How might the combination of image and headline affect readers?
options: The image may suggest distress that the headline does not, creating a mixed or emotional impression
It makes the story purely factual
It proves the protest was violent
It removes all bias
questions.explanation: Image and text can send different signals. Noticing mismatches helps you judge how a multimodal text frames events.

note:
## What is a multimodal text?
A multimodal text communicates through more than one mode. Modes include written language, still images, moving images, colour, layout, typography, gesture and sound. Adverts, posters, websites, cartoons, infographics, film trailers and social media posts are all multimodal. In the MYP, you are expected to explain how these modes work together to create meaning for a particular audience.

## Key visual features
- **Images and composition**: what is shown, how big it is, where it sits, and what is in the foreground or background.
- **Camera angle**: a low angle makes a subject look powerful, a high angle makes them look small, and eye level feels neutral.
- **Shot distance**: a close-up shows emotion or detail, a long shot shows setting and scale.
- **Gaze**: a subject looking directly at the viewer creates a connection (a demand), while looking away invites observation.
- **Colour**: warm colours (red, orange, yellow) often suggest energy, warmth or danger; cool colours (blue, green) suggest calm, trust or nature; dark colours can feel serious or threatening; bright colours attract attention.
- **Typography**: font style, size, boldness and capital letters show tone and importance.
- **Layout and hierarchy**: the order in which the eye moves across the page. Large, central or top items are read first.
- **White space**: empty areas can suggest calm, elegance or focus.

## Language in multimodal texts
Words still matter. Slogans use short punchy phrases, alliteration and imperatives. Captions steer how we read an image. Small print can reveal or hide important details. Always examine how the words and the images interact: do they reinforce each other, add new information, or create irony by contrasting?

## Symbols and visual metaphor
Images can represent ideas. A tap pouring money, a wall, a ladder, a bird in a cage and a rising sun can all have symbolic meaning. Cartoons often use exaggeration and caricature to make a point. As with written metaphors, ask: what idea does this image stand for, and why is it effective?

## Writing about visual texts
Use a clear chain: **feature, description, effect, purpose**. For example, in an invented water campaign poster: "The single drop at the centre of the page is a focal point, and the cool blue background suggests water and calm. Together they draw attention to the slogan and support the message of saving water." Mention audience too: a poster for teenagers might use bold colours and informal slogans, while a bank leaflet may use calm colours and formal language.

## Common mistakes
- Describing the picture without explaining its effect.
- Treating colours as always meaning one thing. Meaning depends on context.
- Ignoring the words, or ignoring the layout.
- Forgetting to link the design to the purpose and audience.
- Missing what is deliberately small or hidden.

## How this is examined
On-screen tasks often show or describe a poster, advert or web page in words and ask how design choices persuade the audience or what impression they give. In multiple choice, you may be asked to match features to effects or to pick the strongest explanation of a design choice. Good answers refer to specific details and explain why they were chosen.

Exam tip: For every visual feature you mention, add the word "because" and explain the effect on the viewer and how that helps the text's purpose.

flashcards.back: A text that combines two or more modes, such as words, images, colour, layout and sound.
A shot taken from below the subject, making them look powerful or dominant.
A shot that fills the frame with a face or object to show emotion or detail.
A subject looking straight at the viewer, creating a personal connection or sense of address.
The order in which the eye reads elements, shaped by size, position, colour and boldness.
Cool colours (blue, green) often suggest calm, trust or nature; warm ones (red, orange) suggest energy, warmth or danger.
An image used to represent an idea, such as a tap pouring money into a tiny cup to show unfair funding.
Explains or steers the reading of an image and can change how the viewer interprets it.
Feature, description, effect on the viewer, then link to purpose and audience.
